---
title: "General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes"
---

## Introduction {#sec-genlik-intro}

The four preceding chapters built multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) on a single integral. An
individual in an aggregate-data (AgD) study is invisible: we never see the patient's covariate vector
$\mathbf{x}$, only the study's reported covariate distribution $f_j$. To place an individual-level outcome
model in the same network as that study, we average the individual model over $f_j$. For a generalized
linear model (GLM) the object that gets averaged is the conditional mean $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$,
and the aggregate-level mean is $\bar\theta_{jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}$ (@thm-aggregation). Chapter 20 showed this average is exact on the identity link
(@thm-identity-link-exact), is the moment generating function on the log link (@thm-log-link-mgf), and has
no closed form on the logit link (@thm-logit-no-closed-form); Chapter 22 then computed the intractable
cases by quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) on a Sobol' net (@def-sobol-net, @thm-hypercube-integration) with a
Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-sklar) to encode covariate dependence. Chapters 23 and 24
established the estimands and the Bayesian computation. All of this was carried out for outcomes that fit
a one-parameter GLM: continuous, binary, and count.

Health-technology-assessment (HTA) practice is dominated by outcomes that do not fit a one-parameter GLM.
The single most common primary endpoint in oncology submissions is **time to an event**, recorded as a
possibly right-censored survival time; cardiovascular and respiratory submissions add composite
time-to-event endpoints; dermatology, oncology, and psychiatry report **ordered categorical** severity
scales (the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index response bands, the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group
performance status, ordinal pain scales). A survival outcome is not summarized by a single mean: it is a
whole curve, and its natural model lives on the hazard, an object indexed by time as well as by
covariates. An ordered categorical outcome is a vector of cell probabilities tied together by a
monotonicity constraint. Neither is a member of the exponential-dispersion family on which Chapters 20 to
23 were built. The question this chapter answers is whether ML-NMR is confined to that family, or whether
the aggregation principle is deeper than the GLM that first carried it.

It is deeper. The aggregation in @thm-aggregation never used the GLM structure of the integrand for
anything except naming it a mean. What the method actually requires is one ingredient: an
**individual-level conditional likelihood**, a function $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\boldsymbol\theta(
\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi))$ giving the probability (or density) of the outcome $y$ for a patient with
covariates $\mathbf{x}$ under parameters $\boldsymbol\xi$. Given that one object, the marginal likelihood
of an AgD individual whose covariates are unobserved is the average of the conditional likelihood over the
study's covariate distribution, and the arm likelihood is the product of these marginal contributions
over the (possibly reconstructed) individuals on the arm. This is the **general-likelihood ML-NMR**
framework of @phillippo2025general, and it extends ML-NMR to any outcome with a parametric individual
model without changing the method. Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18) and simulated
treatment comparison (Chapter 19) also handle survival and ordinal outcomes, through weighted survival fits
and standardized outcome regressions, but each outcome type needs its own weighted or standardized
estimator, and both remain pairwise comparisons in the comparator population.

This chapter develops the framework with survival as the leading and hardest case. We define the survival
function (@def-survival-function) and hazard (@def-hazard) and prove the identity
$S=\exp(-\int h)$ that lets the hazard parameterize the entire distribution
(@thm-survival-hazard-relation). We then expose the feature that makes survival genuinely different from a
GLM: under a proportional-hazards model the conditional log hazard ratio is a clean time-invariant linear
function of the covariates (@thm-conditional-loghr-ph), yet the *marginal* hazard ratio one would estimate
from a population is time-varying even when the conditional model is proportional
(@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying), a survival-scale instance of the non-collapsibility of Chapter 7
(@def-non-collapsibility). The restricted mean survival time (@def-rmst) repairs the collapsibility defect
(@thm-rmst-collapsible) at the price of a transportability subtlety we flag for Chapter 26. We derive the
right-censored individual likelihood (@def-censored-likelihood) from first principles under independent
censoring (@prp-censored-likelihood-density), then build the two aggregation theorems that are the heart
of the chapter: the marginal individual likelihood (@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood) and the aggregate
arm likelihood (@thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood), both resting on @thm-aggregation. The
proportional-odds model (@def-proportional-odds) supplies the ordered-categorical case, and the
general-likelihood theorem (@thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr) unifies everything: one integral, any outcome.
A fully worked exponential-hazard example, in which every survival probability, every marginal hazard,
the restricted mean, and the aggregate likelihood can be checked by hand, closes the development. This
chapter corresponds to results J.1 to J.8 of the proof catalogue.

Throughout, $T\ge 0$ denotes a time-to-event random variable, $S$, $h$, and $H$ its survival, hazard, and
cumulative-hazard functions, and $g$ the link function (@def-link-function) on whose scale the linear
predictor $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd) is built. A population $\mathcal{P}$ is a
distribution over the covariate space $\mathcal{X}$ with density $f_{\mathcal{P}}$; $f_j$ is the
covariate density of study $j$; $\boldsymbol\xi$ is the full parameter vector. We write
$L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i)$ for an individual likelihood contribution and $\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi)$ for
the contribution of arm $k$ of an AgD study $j$.

## The core idea and a running example {#sec-genlik-core-idea}

Before any measure theory, here is the entire method in four sentences, together with one small trial to
hold onto. Every abstract object in this chapter has a concrete counterpart in that trial, and every
theorem below is an elaboration of one of these four steps. A reader who remembers only this section still
has the essential idea.

::: {.remark}
**The general-likelihood recipe, in four steps.**

1. *One patient, covariates known.* Write the likelihood of the outcome for a single patient as if their
covariates $\mathbf{x}$ were observed: choose a conditional individual likelihood
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\text{parameters at }\mathbf{x})$. For a binary outcome this is the Bernoulli
mass; for survival it is the censored kernel $h^{\delta}S$; for an ordinal scale it is a category
probability.
2. *One patient, covariates unknown.* In an aggregate-data (AgD) study the patient's $\mathbf{x}$ was never
recorded, so average the conditional likelihood over the study's reported covariate distribution $f_j$.
This single integral is the whole population adjustment.
3. *Whole arm.* Multiply those averaged contributions across the patients (or reconstructed
pseudo-patients) on the arm.
4. *Whole network.* Share the treatment-effect parameters across studies, so every study estimates the
same relative effects on one linear-predictor scale.

Steps 1 and 3 are ordinary likelihood bookkeeping; step 2 is the population adjustment that makes the AgD
study comparable to the individual-level ones; step 4 is what makes it a network rather than a collection
of separate models. Chapters 20 to 23 carried out these four steps for continuous, binary, and count
outcomes. This chapter proves they go through unchanged for survival and ordered categorical outcomes, and
states the theorem (@thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr) that makes "unchanged" precise. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-genlik-running}
## A running two-arm myeloma trial
Throughout the chapter we follow one small oncology example, a stylized version of the multiple-myeloma
progression-free-survival network of @phillippo2025general. A single binary baseline covariate
$X\in\{0,1\}$ marks a high-risk cytogenetic subgroup, present in half the comparator population,
$P(X=1)=q=\tfrac12$. The endpoint is time to progression $T$, in years, modeled with a constant
(exponential) conditional hazard. On the control arm $C$,
$$
h_C(s\mid x)=\lambda_x,\qquad \lambda_0=1,\quad \lambda_1=3\ \ \text{events per year},
$$
so a high-risk patient has triple the event rate of a standard-risk patient. Treatment $A$ acts by
proportional hazards with a covariate-independent hazard ratio $\psi=\tfrac12$: it halves every patient's
hazard, $h_A(s\mid x)=\tfrac12\lambda_x$, with no effect modification. This conditional model is as clean as
a generalized linear model. The lesson of the chapter is that its *marginal* summaries nonetheless
misbehave (the marginal hazard ratio drifts with time, @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying) while its
aggregate-data likelihood requires a genuine integral (@thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr). We revisit this
trial after every definition and complete the full computation in @exm-genlik-survival. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The survival-specific symbols of the chapter, each shown on the running trial, are collected here for
reference; the abbreviations expand as usual (AgD, aggregate data; IPD, individual patient data).

| Symbol | Name | Meaning | Running trial |
|---|---|---|---|
| $S(t\mid x)$ | survival function | chance of surviving event-free past $t$ | $e^{-\lambda_x t}$ |
| $h(t\mid x)$ | hazard | instantaneous event rate among survivors | constant $\lambda_x$ |
| $H(t\mid x)$ | cumulative hazard | accumulated risk $\int_0^t h$ | $\lambda_x t$ |
| $f(t\mid x)$ | density | event-time density $h\,S$ | $\lambda_x e^{-\lambda_x t}$ |
| $\delta$ | event indicator | $1$ event, $0$ right-censored | per patient |
| $G(t\mid x)$ | censoring survival | chance the censoring time exceeds $t$ | nuisance, cancels |
| $\psi$ | conditional hazard ratio | ratio of conditional hazards | $0.5$, constant |
| $\mathrm{mHR}(s)$ | marginal hazard ratio | ratio of population-averaged hazards | time-varying |
| $\operatorname{RMST}(\tau)$ | restricted mean survival | area under $S$ up to horizon $\tau$ | $\int_0^{\tau}S$ |
| pseudo-IPD | | patient rows reconstructed from a Kaplan-Meier curve | @exm-genlik-survival |

## The survival function and the hazard {#sec-genlik-survival}

A time-to-event outcome is described equivalently by its distribution function, its survival function, its
density, or its hazard. The hazard is the modeling target because it is the scale on which the standard
proportional-hazards and accelerated-failure-time models are linear, and on which the network's relative
effects are reported.

In plain terms, the plan of this section is: define these four equivalent descriptions of a time-to-event
outcome, prove that the hazard alone determines all the others (so a model placed on the hazard is
automatically a complete model of the outcome), and read off the censored likelihood the network will
consume. Keep the running trial in view throughout: the control hazard there is the single number
$\lambda_x$, and we will watch every survival probability, density, and cumulative risk flow from it.

::: {#def-survival-function}
## Survival function
Let $T\ge 0$ be a time-to-event random variable with cumulative distribution function $F_T$. The
**survival function** of $T$ is
$$
S(t):=P(T>t)=1-F_T(t),\qquad t\ge 0,
$$ {#eq-genlik-survival-def}
and, given a covariate vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}$, the **conditional survival function** is
$S(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=P(T>t\mid \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})$. The survival function is non-increasing and
right-continuous, with $\lim_{t\to-\infty}$ replaced by $S(0^-)=1$; for a *continuous* $T$ it is
continuous with $S(0)=1$, and for a *proper* distribution (one with $P(T<\infty)=1$) it satisfies
$\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=0$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** $S(t)$ is just the probability that a patient has not yet had the event by time
$t$. It starts at $S(0)=1$, everyone event-free at enrollment, and decays toward $0$. The three properties
it inherits from the cumulative distribution function of Chapter 4, stated inline so that no back-reference
is needed, are: $S$ is non-increasing (the chance of surviving longer can only fall as the horizon grows),
right-continuous, and runs from $S(0)=1$ down to $\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=0$ for a proper distribution
(everyone eventually has the event). We take these as given rather than reprove them. In the running trial
$S_C(t\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x t}$, so the one-year survival is $e^{-1}=0.37$ for a standard-risk control
patient ($\lambda_0=1$) and $e^{-3}=0.05$ for a high-risk one ($\lambda_1=3$): the high-risk stratum is
depleted far faster. The companion object is the instantaneous event rate among survivors.

::: {#def-hazard}
## Hazard function and cumulative hazard
Let $T$ be a continuous time-to-event variable with density $f$ and survival $S$, and fix $t$ with
$S(t)>0$. The **hazard function** is
$$
h(t):=\lim_{\Delta t\downarrow 0}\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t\mid T\ge t)}{\Delta t}
=\frac{f(t)}{S(t)},
$$ {#eq-genlik-hazard-def}
The second equality $h=f/S$, the working form used throughout, is derived in the proof immediately below.
Conditionally on covariates $h(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=f(t\mid\mathbf{x})/S(t\mid\mathbf{x})$. The
**cumulative hazard** is
$$
H(t):=\int_0^t h(s)\,ds,\qquad H(t\mid\mathbf{x}):=\int_0^t h(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,ds .
$$ {#eq-genlik-cumhaz-def}
The quantity $h(t\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Delta t$ is, to first order in $\Delta t$, the conditional probability
of an event in the next short interval $[t,t+\Delta t)$ given survival to $t$; the hazard is the local
*intensity* of failure, a rate, not a probability, and it can exceed $1$. A hazard of $0.2$ per year does
not mean a $20\%$ chance over all follow-up; it means that among patients still event-free at time $t$, a
fraction of about $0.2\,\Delta t$ have the event in the next interval of length $\Delta t$ years, so
roughly $2\%$ in the next month. In the running trial the constant control hazard is $\lambda_0=1$ per year
for a standard-risk patient and $\lambda_1=3$ per year for a high-risk one; the latter exceeds $1$ and is
still a perfectly valid rate. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.proof}
We verify the second equality in @eq-genlik-hazard-def, which is the working form. By the definition of
conditional probability and continuity of $T$,
$$
\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t\mid T\ge t)}{\Delta t}
=\frac{P(t\le T<t+\Delta t)}{\Delta t\,P(T\ge t)}
=\frac{F_T(t+\Delta t)-F_T(t)}{\Delta t}\cdot\frac{1}{S(t)} ,
$$
using $P(T\ge t)=P(T>t)=S(t)$ for continuous $T$. As $\Delta t\downarrow 0$ the first factor tends to
$F_T'(t)=f(t)$ at every point of differentiability of $F_T$, so the limit is $f(t)/S(t)$. $\square$
:::

The hazard is not merely one summary among several; it determines the distribution completely. This is the
identity on which every parametric and semiparametric survival model rests, and it is the reason a model
specified on the hazard scale yields a coherent likelihood.

Before the formal statement, the idea in one line: the hazard *accumulates* over time into the cumulative
hazard $H(t)=\int_0^t h$, and survival is the exponential of the negative accumulated risk, $S=e^{-H}$. A
patient survives past $t$ exactly to the extent that the risk piled up over $[0,t]$ is small. The theorem
makes this precise and, crucially, invertible: knowing the hazard at every time is the same as knowing the
whole distribution, so a model that specifies the hazard has specified everything.

::: {#thm-survival-hazard-relation}
## The survival function is the exponential of minus the cumulative hazard
Let $T$ be a continuous time-to-event variable whose survival function $S$ is absolutely continuous with
$S(0)=1$, and let $h=f/S$ and $H(t)=\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$ be its hazard and cumulative hazard. Then for every
$t\ge 0$ with $S(t)>0$,
$$
S(t)=\exp\!\Big(-\!\int_0^t h(s)\,ds\Big)=e^{-H(t)},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
H(t)=-\log S(t).
$$ {#eq-genlik-S-exp-H}
The same identity holds conditionally on covariates, $S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-H(t\mid\mathbf{x}))$.
Conversely, any measurable $h\ge 0$ that is locally integrable with $\int_0^\infty h=\infty$ defines,
through @eq-genlik-S-exp-H, a survival function of a proper continuous distribution with density
$f=h\,S$; thus the hazard and the distribution are in one-to-one correspondence.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Forward direction.* Fix $t_0\ge 0$ with $S(t_0)>0$. Because $S$ is non-increasing, $S(s)\ge S(t_0)>0$
for all $s\in[0,t_0]$, so $S$ is bounded away from zero on $[0,t_0]$. Since $S$ is absolutely continuous,
so is $\log S$ on $[0,t_0]$: the logarithm is continuously differentiable on the compact interval
$[S(t_0),1]$, which contains the range of $S$ over $[0,t_0]$, hence Lipschitz there, and a Lipschitz
function composed with an absolutely continuous function is absolutely continuous. (Reminder for the
reader meeting these words: a function is *absolutely continuous* when it is the integral of its own
derivative, which is exactly the property that makes the fundamental theorem of calculus apply to it; it is
*Lipschitz* on a set when the ratio of output change to input change stays bounded there. The logarithm has
derivative $1/u$, which is bounded on $[S(t_0),1]$ because $u$ never drops below $S(t_0)>0$, so it is
Lipschitz there, and feeding an absolutely continuous input into a Lipschitz function preserves absolute
continuity.) An absolutely continuous function is the integral of its almost-everywhere derivative (the
fundamental theorem of calculus for the Lebesgue integral). At every point $s$ where $S$ is differentiable, differentiate the relation $S=1-F_T$ term by term: since
the density is the derivative of the cumulative distribution function, $F_T'=f$ almost everywhere
(Chapter 4), the constant $1$ differentiates to $0$, and $S'(s)=-F_T'(s)=-f(s)$ almost everywhere. Hence
$$
\frac{d}{ds}\log S(s)=\frac{S'(s)}{S(s)}=-\frac{f(s)}{S(s)}=-h(s)
\qquad\text{for almost every }s\in[0,t_0].
$$
Integrating from $0$ to $t_0$ and using $\log S(0)=\log 1=0$,
$$
\log S(t_0)=\log S(0)-\int_0^{t_0}h(s)\,ds=-H(t_0),
$$
and exponentiating gives $S(t_0)=e^{-H(t_0)}$. As $t_0$ was arbitrary subject to $S(t_0)>0$, this is
@eq-genlik-S-exp-H. The conditional statement is identical with $\mathbf{x}$ carried throughout, since for
each fixed $\mathbf{x}$ the function $s\mapsto S(s\mid\mathbf{x})$ is an absolutely continuous survival
function.

*Converse.* Let $h\ge 0$ be locally integrable. Then $H(t)=\int_0^t h$ is non-decreasing, absolutely
continuous, with $H(0)=0$, so $S:=e^{-H}$ is non-increasing, absolutely continuous, $S(0)=1$, and
$\lim_{t\to\infty}S(t)=e^{-\lim H(t)}=e^{-\infty}=0$ under the stated divergence
$\int_0^\infty h=\infty$. Hence $S$ is the survival function of a proper continuous distribution. Its
density is $f=-S'=H'\,e^{-H}=h\,e^{-H}=h\,S$ almost everywhere, and $f/S=h$ recovers the prescribed
hazard. The map $h\mapsto S$ and its inverse $S\mapsto h=-(\log S)'$ are mutually inverse, giving the
one-to-one correspondence. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the hazard scale.** Identity @eq-genlik-S-exp-H is what lets a model place its structure on the
hazard and still deliver a likelihood. Specify $h(t\mid\mathbf{x})$, integrate to $H(t\mid\mathbf{x})$,
exponentiate to $S(t\mid\mathbf{x})$, and the density $f=h\,S$ and the censored likelihood of
@def-censored-likelihood follow. A constant hazard $h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})$ gives the
exponential model $S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=e^{-\lambda(\mathbf{x})t}$; a power-law hazard
$h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\nu t^{\nu-1}$ gives the Weibull model
$S=e^{-\lambda(\mathbf{x})t^{\nu}}$; a flexible spline on $\log h_0$ gives the M-spline baseline used by
the `multinma` survival models of @phillippo2025general. In the running trial the control hazard is the
constant $\lambda_x$, so $H_C(t\mid x)=\lambda_x t$ and $S_C(t\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x t}$: the entire
time-to-progression distribution of each stratum is pinned down by the single number $\lambda_x$, which is
exactly what a one-parameter exponential model asserts. All share the relation
@eq-genlik-S-exp-H. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This pair of definitions and the identity correspond to J.1, J.2, and J.3 in the proof catalogue.

## The conditional and marginal hazard ratio {#sec-genlik-hazard-ratio}

The relative effect in a survival network is reported on the log-hazard scale, so the link is $g=\log$
applied to the hazard. Why that scale? Because the Cox proportional-hazards model is the lingua franca of
oncology and cardiovascular submissions: trials report hazard ratios, regulators and reimbursement agencies
expect them, and the log-hazard is the scale on which those ratios are additive and, as we are about to
see, the scale on which the network's shared effect is a single transportable number. The
proportional-hazards (PH) model writes the conditional hazard as a baseline function modulated by the
exponential of a linear predictor.

::: {.remark}
**The proportional-hazards ML-NMR model.** For an individual with covariates $\mathbf{x}$ in study $j$ on
treatment arm $k$, the PH model is
$$
h_{jk}(s\mid\mathbf{x})=h_{0j}(s)\,\exp\!\big(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})\big),
\qquad
\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k},
$$ {#eq-genlik-ph}
with reference-treatment constraints $\gamma_1=0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\mathbf{0}$. Here
$h_{0j}(s)>0$ is the study-$j$ **baseline hazard**, $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ the prognostic
effect, $\gamma_k$ the treatment main effect, and $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ the
treatment-by-covariate interaction (effect modification). On the log-hazard scale the model is linear,
$\log h_{jk}(s\mid\mathbf{x})=\log h_{0j}(s)+\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$; the scalar study intercept $\mu_j$ of
the GLM notation is here promoted to the baseline log-hazard *function* $\log h_{0j}(s)$, the one feature
that distinguishes survival from a fixed-mean GLM. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Each study keeps its own baseline; the network shares only the effects.** The subscript $j$ on
$h_{0j}(s)$ is load-bearing. Every study is allowed its own baseline hazard function, exactly as every
study in a logistic or normal meta-analysis is allowed its own intercept $\mu_j$. What the network borrows
across studies is not the baseline risk, which reflects each trial's population, accrual, and follow-up,
but the *relative* quantities: the treatment main effects $\gamma_k$ and the effect-modifier interactions
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$. This is the survival analogue of the fixed-study-intercept, shared-treatment-effect
structure used throughout Parts III and V: a nuisance baseline per study, common effects across the network.
It is why a study contributing only a control arm still informs the network (through its baseline and any
prognostic terms) without pinning down a treatment effect on its own. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-conditional-loghr-ph}
## Conditional log hazard ratio under proportional hazards
Under the PH model @eq-genlik-ph, the conditional hazard ratio of treatment $b$ versus treatment $a$ at
covariate value $\mathbf{x}$ is, for every time $s$,
$$
\frac{h_{b}(s\mid\mathbf{x})}{h_{a}(s\mid\mathbf{x})}
=\exp\!\big(\eta_{b}(\mathbf{x})-\eta_{a}(\mathbf{x})\big),
\qquad
\log\frac{h_{b}(s\mid\mathbf{x})}{h_{a}(s\mid\mathbf{x})}
=(\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a}).
$$ {#eq-genlik-cond-loghr}
The conditional log hazard ratio is therefore (i) **time-invariant**, free of $s$, and (ii) **affine in
$\mathbf{x}$**, with slope the difference of interaction vectors. It does not depend on the prognostic
term $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ or on the baseline hazard $h_{0j}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Both arms share the same baseline hazard $h_{0j}(s)$ and prognostic term within a study, so by
@eq-genlik-ph,
$$
\frac{h_b(s\mid\mathbf{x})}{h_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})}
=\frac{h_{0j}(s)\exp(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_b+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b})}
{h_{0j}(s)\exp(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_a+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})} .
$$
The positive factor $h_{0j}(s)$ cancels, eliminating all dependence on $s$, and the common prognostic
factor $\exp(\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1)$ cancels. What remains is
$\exp\big((\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})\big)$. Taking
logarithms gives @eq-genlik-cond-loghr. Both stated properties are immediate from this expression: there
is no $s$, and the dependence on $\mathbf{x}$ is linear. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Because the conditional log hazard ratio is free of time and free of the baseline, one
comparison in the network is described by a single contrast $\gamma_b-\gamma_a$ (plus interaction terms if
there is effect modification), not by a whole time-varying curve. That is precisely what lets a survival
network report one transportable number per treatment comparison, the same kind of estimand the Bucher and
network-meta-analysis machinery of Part III reported on the log-odds and log-rate scales. Take the property
away and there is no single "the effect of $b$ versus $a$" to pool.

The conditional log hazard ratio is thus exactly the kind of object the network models: a contrast of
linear predictors, with effect modification carried by $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$, identifiable from any IPD
arm with enough events by partial likelihood (Cox) or by full parametric likelihood. The marginal hazard
ratio, the quantity a single Cox fit to a population would report, is a different and far less docile
animal. We first record the representation that drives everything.

::: {.remark}
**Conditional versus marginal, in plain language.** A *conditional* hazard ratio compares two treatments
for patients with the *same* covariate value $\mathbf{x}$: it is what a covariate-adjusted Cox model
estimates, and under proportional hazards it is the single number of @thm-conditional-loghr-ph. A
*marginal* hazard ratio compares the two treatments at the level of whole populations, with covariates
averaged out: it is what an *unadjusted* Cox model, fitted to a whole trial arm, reports. One might expect
these to coincide, as they would for a straight-line model. They do not. The reason is survivor selection:
at any time $s>0$ the patients still at risk are not a random sample of the enrolled population but the ones
who have not yet had the event, and treatment changes *who* survives. The marginal hazard ratio at time $s$
therefore compares two differently selected risk sets, and it drifts with $s$ even when the conditional
ratio is a fixed constant. The next lemma makes "averaged over the survivors" exact; the theorem after it
shows the drift cannot be avoided. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-survivor-weighted-hazard}
## Survivor-weighted representation of the marginal hazard
Let $\mathcal{P}$ have covariate density $f_{\mathcal{P}}$, let the conditional hazard
$s\mapsto h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})$ be continuous for each $\mathbf{x}$, and suppose that for every finite
horizon $\Sigma$ the envelope $\sup_{s\le\Sigma}h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})$ is $f_{\mathcal{P}}$-integrable in
$\mathbf{x}$. Define the population (marginal) survival under treatment $t$ as the covariate average
$S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{\mathcal{P}}}[S_t(s\mid\mathbf{X})]$ and the marginal
hazard $h_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s):=-\partial_s\log S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)$. Then
$$
h_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\frac{\int h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}}{\int S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}}
=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_t(\cdot\mid s)}\!\big[h_t(s\mid\mathbf{X})\big],
$$ {#eq-genlik-survivor-rep}
where
$$
\tilde f_t(\mathbf{x}\mid s):=\frac{f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})}
{S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)}
$$ {#eq-genlik-survivor-density}
is the **survivor covariate density**, the distribution of covariates among those still at risk at time $s$
under treatment $t$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-survival-hazard-relation, $\partial_s S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})=-h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,
S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})$. The integrability envelope and $S_t\le 1$ give a dominating function
$\sup_{s\le\Sigma}h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})$ for the integrand $|\partial_s S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})|$ uniformly on
$[0,\Sigma]$, so by the dominated-convergence justification for differentiating under the integral sign
(@thm-dominated-convergence),
$$
\partial_s S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\int\partial_s S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}=-\int h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
$$
Dividing by $S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\int S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$ and
negating yields the first equality in @eq-genlik-survivor-rep. The integrand of the numerator is
$h_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})$ times the density @eq-genlik-survivor-density, so the ratio is the expectation of
$h_t(s\mid\mathbf{X})$ under $\tilde f_t(\cdot\mid s)$. $\square$
:::

The representation says the marginal hazard at time $s$ is the conditional hazard averaged not over the
original population but over the **survivors**, whose covariate distribution $\tilde f_t(\cdot\mid s)$
drifts with $s$. This drift is the engine of non-collapsibility.

::: {.remark}
**A numeric snapshot of survivor drift (running trial).** Take the control arm of the running trial at
$s=0.5$ years. The survivor covariate density @eq-genlik-survivor-density reweights each stratum by its
survival, so the high-risk fraction among survivors is
$$
\tilde f_C(x{=}1\mid 0.5)=\frac{\tfrac12\,e^{-\lambda_1(0.5)}}{\tfrac12\,e^{-\lambda_0(0.5)}+\tfrac12\,
e^{-\lambda_1(0.5)}}=\frac{e^{-1.5}}{e^{-0.5}+e^{-1.5}}=\frac{0.223}{0.607+0.223}=0.269,
$$
down from $0.5$ at enrollment, because high-risk patients have progressed faster. The marginal hazard is
then the survivor-weighted average of the two conditional hazards,
$$
h_C^{\mathcal{P}}(0.5)=0.731\,\lambda_0+0.269\,\lambda_1=0.731(1)+0.269(3)=1.538,
$$
strictly below the enrollment-population average $\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(3)=2$. The population's apparent
hazard fell not because any individual's hazard changed, each stratum keeps its constant $\lambda_x$, but
because the sickest patients have been selected out of the risk set. Repeating this in both arms and at
several times gives the drift of the covariate mix, the "moving picture" of survivor selection:

| time $s$ (years) | high-risk fraction, control $\tilde f_C(1\mid s)$ | high-risk fraction, treated $\tilde f_A(1\mid s)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0$ | $0.500$ | $0.500$ |
| $0.5$ | $0.269$ | $0.378$ |
| $2$ | $0.018$ | $0.119$ |

At every time past $0$ the treated arm still holds relatively more high-risk patients than the control arm,
because treatment $A$ slowed their progression: the two arms are comparing increasingly different covariate
mixes. This is the entire mechanism, and the next theorem shows it forces the marginal hazard ratio to
move. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The theorem below turns this picture into an inequality. Its practical consequence is blunt: a single
marginal hazard ratio read off a Cox fit is an artifact of the follow-up window and the censoring pattern,
not a parameter that transports across trials, populations, or follow-up lengths.

::: {#thm-marginal-hr-time-varying}
## The marginal hazard ratio is time-varying under conditional proportional hazards
Work in a population $\mathcal{P}$ with a covariate that acts as a **frailty** (here meaning a multiplicative
prognostic factor $\rho(\mathbf{x})$ that scales the baseline hazard; we use the word loosely, *not* in the
sense of an unobserved random-effect frailty distribution): there is a measurable
$\rho:\mathcal{X}\to(0,\infty)$, non-degenerate under $f_{\mathcal{P}}$, and a baseline
$h_{a0}(s)>0$ such that the control hazard is $h_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})=h_{a0}(s)\,\rho(\mathbf{x})$, and let
treatment $b$ satisfy conditional proportional hazards with covariate-independent ratio
$h_b(s\mid\mathbf{x})/h_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})=\psi$, a constant with $0<\psi<1$ (a beneficial treatment, no
effect modification on the log-hazard scale). Then the marginal hazard ratio
$$
\mathrm{mHR}(s):=\frac{h_b^{\mathcal{P}}(s)}{h_a^{\mathcal{P}}(s)}
=\psi\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho(\mathbf{X})]}
{\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho(\mathbf{X})]}}_{=:R(s)\ \ge\ 1}
$$ {#eq-genlik-mhr}
satisfies $\mathrm{mHR}(0)=\psi$ and $\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi$ for every $s>0$. Consequently
$\mathrm{mHR}(\cdot)$ is **not constant**: although the conditional hazard ratio is the single number
$\psi$, the marginal hazard ratio varies with time and is attenuated toward the null value $1$. This is
non-collapsibility of the hazard ratio (@def-non-collapsibility) on the survival scale.
:::

::: {.proof}
*The factorization.* Since $h_b=\psi\,h_a$ pointwise, @lem-survivor-weighted-hazard gives
$h_b^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[h_b(s\mid\mathbf{X})]=
\psi\,\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[h_a(s\mid\mathbf{X})]$ and
$h_a^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[h_a(s\mid\mathbf{X})]$. Under the frailty
structure $h_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})=h_{a0}(s)\rho(\mathbf{x})$, the common factor $h_{a0}(s)$ pulls out of both
expectations and cancels in the ratio, leaving @eq-genlik-mhr with
$R(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]/\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]$.

*Value at $s=0$.* From @eq-genlik-survivor-density, $\tilde f_t(\mathbf{x}\mid 0)=f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})
S_t(0\mid\mathbf{x})/S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(0)=f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})$ for both $t\in\{a,b\}$, because
$S_t(0\mid\mathbf{x})=1$. Hence the two survivor distributions coincide with $f_{\mathcal{P}}$ at $s=0$,
$R(0)=1$, and $\mathrm{mHR}(0)=\psi$.

*Strict inequality for $s>0$.* By @thm-survival-hazard-relation and the frailty form,
$S_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-\rho(\mathbf{x})\,A(s))$ with $A(s):=\int_0^s h_{a0}(u)\,du>0$, and
$S_b(s\mid\mathbf{x})=S_a(s\mid\mathbf{x})^{\psi}=\exp(-\psi\rho(\mathbf{x})A(s))$. Therefore the two
survivor densities @eq-genlik-survivor-density are exponential tilts of one another in $\rho$:
$$
\tilde f_a(\mathbf{x}\mid s)\propto f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,e^{-A(s)\rho(\mathbf{x})},
\qquad
\tilde f_b(\mathbf{x}\mid s)\propto f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,e^{-\psi A(s)\rho(\mathbf{x})} ,
$$
so $\tilde f_b\propto\tilde f_a\cdot e^{(1-\psi)A(s)\rho(\mathbf{x})}$ with $(1-\psi)A(s)>0$. (An *exponential
tilt* of a distribution is a reweighting of its density by a factor $e^{c\,\rho(\mathbf{x})}$ followed by
renormalizing; the parameter $c$ is the *natural parameter*, and the family so generated is a one-parameter
exponential family with $\rho$ as its sufficient statistic. So the treated survivor density is an
exponential tilt of the control survivor density.) Introduce the
one-parameter family of tilts $d\mu_c(\mathbf{x})\propto f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,
e^{-A(s)\rho(\mathbf{x})}\,e^{c\,\rho(\mathbf{x})}\,d\mathbf{x}$ for $c\in[0,(1-\psi)A(s)]$, so that
$\mu_0=\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)$ and $\mu_{(1-\psi)A(s)}=\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)$. Let
$m(c):=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_c}[\rho(\mathbf{X})]$. Differentiating the exponential family in its natural
parameter $c$ gives
$$
m'(c)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_c}[\rho^2]-\big(\mathbb{E}_{\mu_c}[\rho]\big)^2
=\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_c}(\rho(\mathbf{X}))\ \ge\ 0,
$$
the last equality being the standard exponential-family identity that the derivative of the mean of the
sufficient statistic with respect to the natural parameter equals its variance (the same score-variance
calculation met for the score function in Chapter 5). The variance is strictly positive because $\rho$ is
non-degenerate under $f_{\mathcal{P}}$ and the tilt keeps the support. Hence $m$ is strictly increasing, so
$\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]=m((1-\psi)A(s))>m(0)=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]$,
that is $R(s)>1$ and $\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi R(s)>\psi$. Because $\psi<1$, moving above $\psi$ moves the
marginal hazard ratio strictly closer to the null $1$. Since $\mathrm{mHR}(0)=\psi\neq\mathrm{mHR}(s)$ for
any $s>0$, $\mathrm{mHR}(\cdot)$ is not constant. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The mechanism, in words.** Treatment $b$ lowers everyone's hazard by the factor $\psi$, so high-frailty
patients survive *longer* under $b$ than under $a$. At any later time the treated risk set therefore still
contains relatively many high-frailty (high-$\rho$) patients, while the control risk set has been depleted
of them; the surviving treated population has a higher average baseline hazard than the surviving control
population. The marginal hazard ratio compares these two differently-selected risk sets and so understates
the true protective effect: it is pulled toward $1$, by more as time passes and selection accumulates. The
conditional model never changed; the marginalization moved. This is precisely the survival-scale form of
the odds-ratio non-collapsibility of @def-non-collapsibility, and it is why a single reported hazard ratio
is an artifact of the follow-up window and the censoring distribution, not a transportable parameter.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

These results correspond to J.4a (@thm-conditional-loghr-ph) and J.4b (@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying) in
the proof catalogue.

## Restricted mean survival time, a collapsible alternative {#sec-genlik-rmst}

The non-collapsibility and time-variation of the marginal hazard ratio motivate a marginal summary that
behaves. The restricted mean survival time is the area under the survival curve up to a fixed horizon; it
is collapsible over covariates by a one-line Fubini argument.

::: {#def-rmst}
## Restricted mean survival time
For a horizon $\tau>0$, the **restricted mean survival time** (RMST) of treatment $t$ in population
$\mathcal{P}$ is
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_t^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau):=\int_0^{\tau}S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)\,ds,
$$ {#eq-genlik-rmst}
the expected event-free time over $[0,\tau]$. The conditional RMST is
$\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid\mathbf{x}):=\int_0^{\tau}S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,ds$, and the **RMST
contrast** of $b$ versus $a$ is
$\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{ab}^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau):=\operatorname{RMST}_b^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)-
\operatorname{RMST}_a^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-rmst-collapsible}
## RMST and the RMST contrast are collapsible over covariates
With $S_t^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{\mathcal{P}}}[S_t(s\mid\mathbf{X})]$,
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_t^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{\mathcal{P}}}\!\big[\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid\mathbf{X})\big],
\qquad
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{ab}^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{\mathcal{P}}}\!\big[\operatorname{RMST}_b(\tau\mid\mathbf{X})
-\operatorname{RMST}_a(\tau\mid\mathbf{X})\big].
$$ {#eq-genlik-rmst-collapse}
The marginal RMST is the population average of the conditional RMSTs: marginal equals average conditional,
which is collapsibility.
:::

::: {.proof}
The integrand $S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\ge 0$ is jointly measurable in $(s,\mathbf{x})$ and nonnegative, so by
Tonelli's theorem (@thm-fubini-tonelli) the order of integration over $s\in[0,\tau]$ (Lebesgue measure)
and over $\mathbf{x}$ (the measure $f_{\mathcal{P}}$) may be exchanged:
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_t^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)=\int_0^{\tau}\!\!\Big(\int S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,
f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\Big)ds
=\int\!\Big(\int_0^{\tau}S_t(s\mid\mathbf{x})\,ds\Big)f_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\big[\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid\mathbf{X})\big].
$$
The contrast statement follows by linearity of expectation applied to the difference of the two arms.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Collapsible but not automatically transportable.** Collapsibility (marginal equals average conditional)
is a statement *within* one population $\mathcal{P}$; transportability is a statement *across*
populations. The RMST contrast is collapsible by @thm-rmst-collapsible, yet if the conditional model is
fitted on the log-hazard scale (PH, $g=\log$) while the reported effect is the RMST (a time-scale
quantity), the composition $\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})=\int_0^{\tau}
\exp\!\big(-\!\int_0^s e^{\eta_t(\mathbf{x})}h_{0}(u)\,du\big)ds$ is a nonlinear functional of
$\eta_t(\mathbf{x})$. Conditional constancy of relative effects (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) is
assumed on the log-hazard scale, not on the RMST scale, so the RMST contrast computed in the comparator
population does not generally equal the RMST contrast in a different target population; transporting it
requires the target covariate distribution and baseline hazard, exactly as in the scale-misalignment
analysis taken up for the unanchored case in Chapter 26
(@thm-mlumr-tte). The clean estimand to transport remains the conditional log-hazard model; RMST is a
collapsible *read-out* in a stated population. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Collapsible does not mean transportable: a two-population snapshot.** It is tempting to hear "collapsible"
and conclude "safe to compare across populations." It is not. Collapsibility says the marginal RMST contrast
in a population equals the average of the conditional contrasts *in that same population*; it says nothing
about a different population with a different covariate mix. In the running trial the conditional RMST
contrast at horizon $\tau=2$ is $0.399$ years for a standard-risk patient ($x=0$) and $0.301$ years for a
high-risk patient ($x=1$) (both computed in @exm-genlik-survival). A comparator population with high-risk
prevalence $q=\tfrac12$ therefore has marginal contrast $\tfrac12(0.399)+\tfrac12(0.301)=0.350$ years,
whereas a target population with $q^{*}=\tfrac14$ has $\tfrac34(0.399)+\tfrac14(0.301)=0.375$ years. Same
conditional model, same treatment, different marginal RMST contrast, purely because the covariate mix
differs. The object that *is* shared across the two populations is the conditional log-hazard model; the
RMST contrast must be recomputed in each target population, which is why transporting it needs the target
covariate distribution. @exr-genlik-rmst-transport works the general formula. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The practical decision rule for a survival submission follows.

| Quantity | Scale | Transports across populations? | Role in the analysis |
|---|---|---|---|
| conditional log-hazard effects $\gamma_k,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ | log-hazard | yes, under conditional constancy of relative effects (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) | the estimand to fit and share across the network |
| marginal hazard ratio $\mathrm{mHR}(s)$ | hazard | no; varies with time and population | not a transportable summary; avoid reporting it as one number |
| RMST contrast $\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{ab}^{\mathcal{P}}(\tau)$ | time | only by recomputing with the target covariate mix and baseline hazard | collapsible read-out; always report with its target population $\mathcal{P}$ and horizon $\tau$ |

In one line: fit and transport on the conditional log-hazard scale, report RMST as a population-specific
read-out, and never treat a single marginal hazard ratio as a transportable parameter.

This result corresponds to J.4c in the proof catalogue.

## The right-censored individual likelihood {#sec-genlik-likelihood}

Survival data are incomplete: for many patients we observe not the event time but a censoring time, the
last moment at which they were known to be event-free. The likelihood must use the density for observed
events and the survival probability for censored observations. We define the contribution and then derive
it from the joint model of event and censoring under the standard independence assumption.

::: {#def-censored-likelihood}
## Right-censored individual likelihood
Let an individual with covariates $\mathbf{x}$ have a (possibly right-censored) observation
$(t,\delta)$, where $t\ge 0$ is the observed time and $\delta\in\{0,1\}$ is the event indicator:
$\delta=1$ if $t$ is an event time and $\delta=0$ if $t$ is a right-censoring time. Under a model with
conditional hazard $h(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$ and survival $S(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x};
\boldsymbol\xi)$, the **right-censored individual likelihood contribution** is
$$
L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;t,\delta,\mathbf{x})
=h(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)^{\delta}\;S(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)
=\begin{cases}
f(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)=h(t\mid\mathbf{x})S(t\mid\mathbf{x}), & \delta=1,\\[2pt]
S(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi), & \delta=0.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-genlik-censored-lik}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation, and a timeline.** Picture one patient's follow-up as a horizontal line beginning at
enrollment. Two things can end the line. If the event (progression) is *observed* at time $t$, we know
exactly when it happened, and the contribution is the density $f(t\mid\mathbf{x})=h(t\mid\mathbf{x})
S(t\mid\mathbf{x})$: the chance of surviving event-free up to $t$, times the instantaneous rate of failing
right at $t$. If instead the patient is last seen event-free at time $t$, because the trial reached its data
cutoff or the patient left for reasons unrelated to prognosis, the line is *right-censored*: we know only
that $T>t$, and the contribution is the survival probability $S(t\mid\mathbf{x})$. An event pins down a
point on the line; a censoring pins down only a lower bound. The single formula $h^{\delta}S$ encodes both
by switching the hazard factor on ($\delta=1$) or off ($\delta=0$). In the running trial we will use exactly
two such patients on the comparator control arm: an event at $t_1=0.5$ years and a censoring at $t_2=2$
years (@exm-genlik-survival, Step 4).

::: {#prp-censored-likelihood-density}
## Derivation of the censored likelihood under independent censoring
Let the event time $T$ have conditional density $f(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$, survival
$S(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$, and hazard $h=f/S$, and let the censoring time $C$ be
conditionally independent of $T$ given $\mathbf{x}$, with survival $G(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x})$ and density
$g(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x})$ that do **not** depend on the event-model parameter $\boldsymbol\xi$
(non-informative, independent censoring). We observe $\tilde T=\min(T,C)$ and
$\delta=\mathbf{1}\{T\le C\}$. Then the joint density of the observed pair $(\tilde t,\delta)$ factorizes
as
$$
p(\tilde t,\delta\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)
=\big[f(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)\,G(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x})\big]^{\delta}
\big[S(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)\,g(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x})\big]^{1-\delta},
$$ {#eq-genlik-joint-censor}
and the factor depending on $\boldsymbol\xi$ is proportional to @eq-genlik-censored-lik. Hence the
maximum-likelihood and Bayesian inferences for $\boldsymbol\xi$ may use $h^{\delta}S$ as the individual
contribution, discarding the censoring factors $G^{\delta}g^{1-\delta}$ as constants in $\boldsymbol\xi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Condition on $\mathbf{x}$ throughout and suppress it; independence of $T$ and $C$ makes their joint
density $f(t)g(c)$. Consider the two observable events.

*An event ($\delta=1$) observed at $\tilde t=t$.* In words, we see an event at $t$ exactly when the true
event time equals $t$ and the censoring time has not yet arrived, that is $C\ge t$; those are the censoring
values compatible with observing the event. This is the set $\{T=t,\ C\ge t\}$, and its density in $t$ is
obtained by integrating the joint density over all such censoring values $c\ge t$ that leave $T$ uncensored:
$$
\int_{t}^{\infty}f(t)\,g(c)\,dc=f(t)\int_t^{\infty}g(c)\,dc=f(t)\,G(t),
$$
using $\int_t^\infty g(c)\,dc=P(C>t)=G(t)$.

*A censoring ($\delta=0$) observed at $\tilde t=c$.* Symmetrically, we see a censoring at $c$ exactly when
the censoring time equals $c$ and the true event has not yet happened, that is $T>c$. This is the set
$\{C=c,\ T>c\}$, with density in $c$
$$
\int_{c}^{\infty}f(t)\,g(c)\,dt=g(c)\int_c^{\infty}f(t)\,dt=g(c)\,S(c).
$$
Writing both cases with the indicator $\delta$ gives @eq-genlik-joint-censor. Substituting
$f=h\,S$ in the $\delta=1$ branch,
$$
p(\tilde t,\delta\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)
=\big[h(\tilde t)S(\tilde t)\big]^{\delta}S(\tilde t)^{1-\delta}\cdot
G(\tilde t)^{\delta}g(\tilde t)^{1-\delta}
=\underbrace{h(\tilde t)^{\delta}S(\tilde t)}_{\text{depends on }\boldsymbol\xi}\cdot
\underbrace{G(\tilde t)^{\delta}g(\tilde t)^{1-\delta}}_{\text{free of }\boldsymbol\xi},
$$
where the exponents of $S$ combine as $\delta+(1-\delta)=1$. The second factor does not involve
$\boldsymbol\xi$, so as a function of $\boldsymbol\xi$ the contribution is proportional to
$h(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta}S(\tilde t\mid\mathbf{x})$, which is @eq-genlik-censored-lik. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Scope of the assumption.** The factorization needs only that censoring is independent of the event time
given covariates and that its mechanism carries no information about $\boldsymbol\xi$. In health-research
terms, three common patterns clarify the boundary. *Administrative censoring* at a common data cutoff, when
the trial database locks on a fixed calendar date, satisfies the assumption, because the cutoff date is
unrelated to any individual patient's prognosis. *Loss to follow-up* satisfies it only when the reason a
patient drops out is unrelated to their event risk after conditioning on covariates, for example a patient
who moves house. *Informative dropout*, where patients leave the study precisely because they are
deteriorating, violates it: then a censoring carries hidden bad news about $T$, the censoring survival $G$
is no longer free of $\boldsymbol\xi$, and the clean split fails. Interval censoring and left truncation
likewise break the split and require the corresponding modified contributions; see the survival-analysis
texts cited in @sec-genlik-notes. For the network the important
point is that @eq-genlik-censored-lik is a *conditional individual likelihood* of exactly the form the
aggregation machinery of the next section consumes. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This corresponds to J.4 in the proof catalogue.

## Aggregation for general likelihoods {#sec-genlik-aggregation}

We now perform the step that makes survival (or any other) outcomes part of an ML-NMR network. In an AgD
study the individual covariate vectors are unobserved, so the conditional likelihood
@eq-genlik-censored-lik cannot be evaluated at a known $\mathbf{x}$. Instead we average it over the
study's covariate distribution. This is the general-likelihood analogue of the mean-aggregation theorem
@thm-aggregation of Chapter 20, and it is what @phillippo2025general call the integrated likelihood.

One question must be settled before the theorems: if the study is *aggregate*, where do the individual
observations $y_{1jk},\dots,y_{n_{jk}jk}$ in the theorems below come from? Two situations arise. When the
outcome has a sufficient summary, a binary study reporting an event count, no individual rows are needed and
the arm likelihood collapses to a single aggregate contribution (Chapters 20 and 21). Survival has no such
single summary: the reported object is a Kaplan-Meier curve. There the individual rows are *pseudo-IPD*,
patient-level times and event indicators reconstructed from the published curve, sketched in the bridge
after @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood and developed in Chapter 26. The point to hold throughout this
section is a split that beginners often miss: even after the event *times* are reconstructed, the
*covariates* are still unobserved. We know when each pseudo-patient progressed or was censored, but not
their covariate vector $\mathbf{x}$; that is exactly why the covariate integral over $f_j$ remains, applied
to every pseudo-patient.

::: {#thm-marginal-individual-likelihood}
## Marginal individual likelihood
Consider an individual $i$ in an AgD study $j$, with outcome $y_i$ observed but covariate vector
$\mathbf{X}_i$ unobserved and distributed according to the study covariate density $f_j$. Let
$L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i,\mathbf{x})$ be the conditional individual likelihood, that is the
conditional density or probability mass $p(y_i\mid\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\xi)$ of the outcome given
covariates (for survival, @eq-genlik-censored-lik; for binary, the Bernoulli mass; and so on). Then the
**marginal individual likelihood**, the likelihood contribution that uses only the observed $y_i$, is
$$
L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i)
=\int_{\mathcal{X}}L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i,\mathbf{x})\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_j}\!\big[\,p(y_i\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol\xi)\,\big].
$$ {#eq-genlik-marginal-lik}
For discrete covariates the integral is a sum over $\mathcal{X}$.
:::

**Intuition.** The aggregate study never recorded $\mathbf{x}$, so we cannot condition on it. The only
honest likelihood for the observed outcome $y_i$ is the one that integrates $\mathbf{x}$ out, weighting each
possible covariate value by how common it is in *that* study, namely $f_j$. That weighted average is
@eq-genlik-marginal-lik. The proof is nothing more than the law of total probability made explicit, but the
modeling content is real: it is step 2 of the recipe of @sec-genlik-core-idea, and it is what makes an AgD
arm comparable to an IPD arm in the same network.

::: {.proof}
Under parameter $\boldsymbol\xi$ the joint law of $(Y_i,\mathbf{X}_i)$ in study $j$ has density
$p(y_i,\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol\xi)=p(y_i\mid\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\xi)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})=
L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i,\mathbf{x})\,f_j(\mathbf{x})$, the conditional outcome model times
the covariate density. The likelihood of the *observed* datum is the marginal density of $Y_i$, obtained
by integrating out the unobserved $\mathbf{X}_i$ (the law of total probability, equivalently
marginalization of a joint density, Chapter 4):
$$
L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i)=p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(y_i,\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,
d\mathbf{x}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i,\mathbf{x})\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x},
$$
which is @eq-genlik-marginal-lik. The integral is finite because $L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}\ge 0$ and, for a
probability-mass outcome, $L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}\le 1$, so the integral is at most $\int f_j=1$; for a
density outcome it is the marginal density of $Y_i$, finite for almost every $y_i$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Relation to mean aggregation and to numerical integration.** @thm-aggregation aggregates the
conditional *mean* $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$; theorem @thm-marginal-individual-likelihood aggregates
the conditional *likelihood* $L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}$. The two agree exactly when the likelihood kernel is
affine in the mean, as for the Bernoulli mass $p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}$, which equals $p$ at $y=1$ and $1-p$ at
$y=0$: then $\int p(\mathbf{x})^{y}(1-p(\mathbf{x}))^{1-y}f_j\,d\mathbf{x}=\bar p^{\,y}(1-\bar p)^{1-y}$
with $\bar p=\int p\,f_j$, so integrating the likelihood reproduces the aggregate-mean model. Contrast the
count case as an explicit *non*-example: the Poisson mass $\theta^{y}e^{-\theta}/y!$ is not affine in its
mean $\theta$ (it carries both a $\theta^{y}$ factor and an $e^{-\theta}$ factor), so in general
$\int \theta(\mathbf{x})^{y}e^{-\theta(\mathbf{x})}/y!\,f_j\,d\mathbf{x}\ne\bar\theta^{y}e^{-\bar\theta}/y!$;
averaging the likelihood is genuinely different from evaluating it at the average mean. The Gaussian
density, the survival kernel $h^{\delta}S$, and the proportional-odds mass $p_k$ of
@def-proportional-odds fail affinity in the same way; for them the integral @eq-genlik-marginal-lik does
not reduce to mean aggregation, and like the logit case (@thm-logit-no-closed-form) it generally has no
closed form. It is then
evaluated by the Sobol' QMC rule of Chapter 22 (@def-sobol-net, @thm-hypercube-integration): with
integration nodes $\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(N)}$ drawn from $f_j$ through the inverse-CDF map
(@thm-inverse-cdf) and a Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-sklar) for covariate dependence,
$$
L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i)\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{r=1}^{N}
L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}\!\big(\boldsymbol\xi;y_i,\mathbf{x}^{(r)}\big),
$$
the same average that drives every AgD contribution in the network. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The arm likelihood is the product of these marginal contributions. We make the conditional-independence
structure explicit so that the product is justified rather than assumed.

::: {#thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood}
## Aggregate arm likelihood
Let arm $k$ of AgD study $j$ contribute $n_{jk}$ individual observations $y_{1jk},\dots,y_{n_{jk}jk}$ whose
unobserved covariate vectors are independent draws from $f_j$, and let the outcomes be conditionally
independent across individuals given their covariates and $\boldsymbol\xi$. Then the marginalized outcomes
$Y_{1jk},\dots,Y_{n_{jk}jk}$ are independent, each with the marginal individual likelihood
@eq-genlik-marginal-lik, and the **aggregate arm likelihood** factorizes as
$$
\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi;\mathbf{y}_{jk})
=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_{ijk})
=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_{ijk},\mathbf{x})\,
f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
$$ {#eq-genlik-aggregate-lik}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1jk},\dots,Y_{n_{jk}jk})$ and $\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}_{1},\dots,
\mathbf{X}_{n_{jk}})$. Conditional independence of outcomes given covariates and $\boldsymbol\xi$ gives the
joint conditional density $p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol\xi)=\prod_{i}p(y_{ijk}\mid\mathbf{X}_i,
\boldsymbol\xi)$, and independence of the covariate draws gives the joint covariate density
$\prod_i f_j(\mathbf{x}_i)$. Marginalizing the covariates from the joint law and using Tonelli's theorem
(@thm-fubini-tonelli) on the nonnegative integrand to factor the multiple integral into a product of
single integrals,
$$
\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi)
=\int_{\mathcal{X}^{n_{jk}}}\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}p(y_{ijk}\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol\xi)\,
f_j(\mathbf{x}_i)\,d\mathbf{x}_1\cdots d\mathbf{x}_{n_{jk}}
=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(y_{ijk}\mid\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\xi)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}
=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}L_i(\boldsymbol\xi;y_{ijk}),
$$
which is @eq-genlik-aggregate-lik. The factorization shows the $Y_{ijk}$ are independent with the stated
marginals. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Sufficient summaries and pseudo-IPD.** When the conditional kernel is affine in a mean and the AgD
report a sufficient summary, @eq-genlik-aggregate-lik collapses to a low-dimensional aggregate model: for
Bernoulli outcomes summarized by an event count $r_{jk}=\sum_i y_{ijk}$, the product is
$\bar p_{jk}^{\,r_{jk}}(1-\bar p_{jk})^{n_{jk}-r_{jk}}$, the binomial likelihood with aggregate success
probability $\bar p_{jk}=\int\operatorname{expit}(\eta_{jk})f_j$, recovering the binary ML-NMR of Chapters
20 and 21 and, with no covariates to integrate, the standard network meta-analysis likelihood
(@thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma). For survival the reported summary is a Kaplan-Meier curve, which is not a
single sufficient statistic; the individual observations entering @eq-genlik-aggregate-lik are then
**pseudo-IPD** $(t_{ijk},\delta_{ijk})$ reconstructed from the published curve and the numbers at risk,
the reconstruction whose validity is established for the unanchored setting in Chapter 26
(@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction). In outline the reconstruction, the algorithm of @guyot2012,
digitizes the published Kaplan-Meier curve into a fine grid of (time, survival-probability) points, then
uses the reported numbers at risk in each interval to solve, step by step, for how many events and how many
censorings must have occurred to produce the observed drops in the curve; its output is a table of
pseudo-observations $(t_{ijk},\delta_{ijk})$ whose own Kaplan-Meier estimate reproduces the published one.
What is recovered is the pair (time, event indicator) for each pseudo-patient; what remains unobserved is
the covariate vector, which is again why each pseudo-patient still contributes the integrated likelihood
@eq-genlik-marginal-lik over $f_j$ rather than a conditional likelihood at a known $\mathbf{x}$. This
digitize-then-reconstruct step is the one part of a real submission that most distinguishes practice from
the clean theory, so we flag it here rather than leaving it entirely to Chapter 26. Once reconstructed, each
pseudo-individual contributes the marginal censored likelihood @eq-genlik-censored-lik integrated over
$f_j$, exactly as in @eq-genlik-aggregate-lik. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

These two theorems correspond to J.5 (@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood) and J.6
(@thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood) in the proof catalogue.

## Ordered categorical outcomes {#sec-genlik-ordinal}

The second outcome type that escapes the one-parameter GLM is the ordered categorical scale, and it is not
a niche case. HTA submissions routinely report ordered severity bands: the Eastern Cooperative Oncology
Group (ECOG) performance status $0,1,2,3,4$, psoriasis response bands (PASI 50, 75, 90), and ordinal pain or
function scales. The categories have a meaningful order, better to worse, but no numeric spacing, so a mean
is not the natural summary; the natural object is the whole vector of category probabilities, tied together
by the order. The standard model is the proportional-odds (cumulative-logit) model, which places a single
linear predictor against an increasing ladder of cutpoints. We develop it, give it the same concrete
two-point treatment the survival case received, and show it drops into the aggregation machinery of
@sec-genlik-aggregation without a single change.

::: {#def-proportional-odds}
## Proportional-odds model
Let $Y\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}$ be an ordered categorical outcome (the categories carry a meaningful order, for
example increasing disease severity). With cutpoints $\alpha_1\le\alpha_2\le\cdots\le\alpha_{K-1}$ and a
linear predictor $\eta(\mathbf{x})$, the **proportional-odds model** specifies the cumulative
probabilities by
$$
\operatorname{logit}P(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})=\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad k=1,\dots,K-1,
$$ {#eq-genlik-po}
equivalently $P(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x}))$. With the
conventions $\alpha_0=-\infty$ and $\alpha_K=+\infty$ (so $\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_0-\eta)=0$ and
$\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_K-\eta)=1$), the **category probabilities** are the consecutive differences
$$
p_k(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi):=P(Y=k\mid\mathbf{x})
=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x}))-\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_{k-1}-\eta(\mathbf{x})),
\qquad k=1,\dots,K.
$$ {#eq-genlik-po-prob}
For ML-NMR (and the unanchored ML-UMR of Chapter 26) the linear predictor is the network linear predictor
$\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$,
with study-specific cutpoints $\alpha_{k}^{(j)}$ permitted. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** Imagine a hidden continuous "severity" axis. The cutpoints
$\alpha_1\le\cdots\le\alpha_{K-1}$ are fixed thresholds that slice this axis into the $K$ ordered
categories, and the linear predictor $\eta(\mathbf{x})$ shifts a patient's position along it. (Recall
$\operatorname{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$, the inverse logit, increasing from $0$ to $1$.) The minus sign in
$\operatorname{logit}P(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x})=\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x})$ is a direction convention: a *larger*
$\eta(\mathbf{x})$ lowers every cumulative probability $P(Y\le k)$, which pushes probability mass toward the
*higher* (worse) categories. So with this convention a positive treatment or covariate effect on $\eta$
means "more severe." The name *proportional odds* refers to the property proved next: the effect of
covariates on the cumulative odds is the *same at every cutpoint* $k$, a single shared slope rather than one
slope per threshold, which is what makes the model parsimonious enough to enter a network with a single
$\eta_{jk}$.

::: {#lem-ordinal-valid-probabilities}
## The proportional-odds category probabilities are a valid distribution; proportional odds
Fix $\mathbf{x}$ and write $p_k=p_k(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$ as in @eq-genlik-po-prob. If the cutpoints
are ordered, $\alpha_1\le\cdots\le\alpha_{K-1}$, then $p_k\ge 0$ for all $k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1$.
Moreover the model has the **proportional-odds property**: for any two covariate values
$\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'$ and any cutpoint $k\in\{1,\dots,K-1\}$, the cumulative log odds ratio
$$
\log\frac{\operatorname{odds}(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x})}{\operatorname{odds}(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x}')}
=\eta(\mathbf{x}')-\eta(\mathbf{x})
$$
does not depend on $k$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Nonnegativity.* The function $\operatorname{expit}$ is strictly increasing. For $1\le k\le K$ the
ordering $\alpha_{k-1}\le\alpha_k$ (including the conventions $\alpha_0=-\infty\le\alpha_1$ and
$\alpha_{K-1}\le+\infty=\alpha_K$) gives $\alpha_{k-1}-\eta(\mathbf{x})\le\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x})$, hence
$\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_{k-1}-\eta)\le\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta)$, so
$p_k=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta)-\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_{k-1}-\eta)\ge 0$.

*Sum to one.* The sum telescopes:
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big[\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta)-\operatorname{expit}
(\alpha_{k-1}-\eta)\Big]=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_K-\eta)-\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_0-\eta)=1-0=1.
$$

*Proportional odds.* From @eq-genlik-po, $\operatorname{logit}P(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x})=
\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x})$, and the logit of a probability is the log odds, so the log odds of $Y\le k$ is
$\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x})$. Subtracting the same expression at $\mathbf{x}'$ cancels the cutpoint
$\alpha_k$:
$$
\log\operatorname{odds}(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x})-\log\operatorname{odds}(Y\le k\mid\mathbf{x}')
=\big(\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x})\big)-\big(\alpha_k-\eta(\mathbf{x}')\big)=\eta(\mathbf{x}')-\eta(\mathbf{x}),
$$
independent of $k$. $\square$
:::

The conditional individual likelihood for an ordered categorical observation $y_i=k$ is simply the
category probability $L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;k,\mathbf{x})=p_k(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$ of
@eq-genlik-po-prob, which is a probability mass in $[0,1]$, so @thm-marginal-individual-likelihood and
@thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood apply verbatim: the marginal individual likelihood of an AgD ordinal
observation is $\int_{\mathcal{X}}p_{k}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$, evaluated
by QMC. Because $p_k$ is not affine in a single mean, this integral, like the survival integral, does not
reduce to mean aggregation.

::: {#exm-genlik-ordinal}
## A three-category performance-status aggregation
Collapse ECOG performance status into three ordered bands $Y\in\{1,2,3\}$ (good, intermediate, poor), and
use the same binary high-risk covariate $X\in\{0,1\}$ as the running survival trial, with prevalence
$q=P(X=1)=\tfrac12$ in the comparator AgD population. Take cutpoints $\alpha_1=-1,\ \alpha_2=1$ and a linear
predictor $\eta(x)=\eta_0+\beta x$ with $\eta_0=0,\ \beta=1$, so $\eta(0)=0$ and $\eta(1)=1$; the high-risk
covariate raises severity.

**Conditional category probabilities.** With
$p_k(x)=\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_k-\eta(x))-\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_{k-1}-\eta(x))$ and
$\operatorname{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
x=0:\quad &P(Y\le1)=\operatorname{expit}(-1)=0.269,\quad P(Y\le2)=\operatorname{expit}(1)=0.731,\\
&(p_1,p_2,p_3)=(0.269,\ 0.462,\ 0.269);\\[2pt]
x=1:\quad &P(Y\le1)=\operatorname{expit}(-2)=0.119,\quad P(Y\le2)=\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.500,\\
&(p_1,p_2,p_3)=(0.119,\ 0.381,\ 0.500).
\end{aligned}
$$
The high-risk covariate ($x=1$) moves mass out of the good band ($p_1:0.269\to0.119$) and into the poor band
($p_3:0.269\to0.500$), exactly the "larger $\eta$ means more severe" direction of the sign convention.
Proportional odds is visible directly: the $x{=}1$ versus $x{=}0$ difference in cumulative log odds is
$\eta(0)-\eta(1)=-1$ at *both* cutpoints (at $k=1$, $(-2)-(-1)=-1$; at $k=2$, $0-1=-1$), one shared slope.

**Marginal (aggregate) category probabilities.** Averaging over $X\sim\operatorname{Ber}(\tfrac12)$, a
two-point sum with weights $\tfrac12,\tfrac12$, gives the integrated category probabilities of an AgD
patient:
$$
\bar p_1=\tfrac12(0.269)+\tfrac12(0.119)=0.194,\quad
\bar p_2=\tfrac12(0.462)+\tfrac12(0.381)=0.421,\quad
\bar p_3=\tfrac12(0.269)+\tfrac12(0.500)=0.384,
$$
which sum to $1$. The marginal individual likelihood of a single AgD observation recorded in the poor band
is $L_i=\bar p_3=0.384$; for the intermediate band it is $\bar p_2=0.421$. These are the ordinal instances of
@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood: the two integration nodes are the covariate values $\{0,1\}$ with QMC
weights $\{\tfrac12,\tfrac12\}$, exactly as in Step 4 of the survival example, and a continuous covariate
would replace the two-point sum with an $N$-node Sobol' average. The aggregate arm likelihood is the product
of such $\bar p_{y_i}$ over the arm's individuals, by @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood. Because $p_k$ is
not affine in a single mean, this integrated likelihood does not collapse to a category probability
evaluated at some aggregate mean; the full two-point (in general $N$-point) average is retained, precisely
as for survival. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**When proportional odds fails.** The single slope $\eta(\mathbf{x})$ shared across cutpoints is an
assumption; it can be assessed and relaxed. Sensitivity models include the adjacent-category logit, the
continuation-ratio model, and the unconstrained multinomial logit; each supplies a different conditional
category-probability kernel $L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}$, and each is aggregated by the identical integral
@eq-genlik-marginal-lik. The generality of the framework is precisely that the choice of ordinal model is
a choice of integrand, not a change of machinery. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This corresponds to J.7 in the proof catalogue.

## The general-likelihood ML-NMR framework {#sec-genlik-general}

We can now state the unifying theorem. Everything above was a special case of a single construction: pick
a conditional individual likelihood, average it over the covariate distribution to aggregate, multiply
over individuals.

Before the statement, a map of its symbols, since several parameter objects appear at once. Each abstract
object corresponds to a concrete item in a submission, illustrated on the running trial.

| Symbol | Name | Plain meaning | Running trial |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)$ | conditional individual likelihood | the outcome model for one patient with known covariates | $h^{\delta}S$, exponential |
| $\boldsymbol\theta$ | conditional parameter | the parameter that outcome model needs (a mean, a hazard, a probability vector) | the hazard $\lambda_x$ |
| $\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$ | network-mapped parameter | how the network builds that parameter from covariates and shared effects | $\psi\lambda_x$ treated, $\lambda_x$ control |
| $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$ | linear predictor | prognostic plus treatment plus interaction terms | the log-hazard shift |
| $\boldsymbol\xi$ | full parameter vector | all unknowns: baselines, prognostic effects, treatment effects, cutpoints | $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\psi)$ |
| $f_j$ | study covariate distribution | the reported covariate mix of study $j$ | $X\sim\operatorname{Ber}(\tfrac12)$ |
| IPD arm | | patient-level rows observed | an individual-level study |
| AgD arm | | only summaries; covariates integrated out | the comparator arm |

Whether the general integral @eq-genlik-general *simplifies* depends entirely on one property of the kernel,
affinity in the mean, summarized in @tbl-genlik-reduction.

| Outcome family | Kernel in the mean $\theta$ | Affine in $\theta$? | Integrated likelihood $=\pi(y\mid\bar\theta_{jk})$? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian, identity link | $e^{-(y-\theta)^2/2\sigma^2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma$ | no | no (a normal mixture; the arm *mean* is still exact, @thm-identity-link-exact) |
| Bernoulli / binomial | $\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{1-y}$ | yes | yes |
| Poisson, count | $\theta^{y}e^{-\theta}/y!$ | no | no |
| Censored survival | $h^{\delta}S$ | no | no |
| Ordered categorical | $p_k$ | no | no |

: Which outcome families collapse to mean aggregation. For the "yes" families the arm likelihood is the
kernel evaluated at the aggregate mean $\bar\theta_{jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_{jk})f_j$; computing
$\bar\theta_{jk}$ may still need quasi-Monte Carlo when the link has no closed-form average (the logit,
@thm-logit-no-closed-form), but the likelihood *structure* collapses. For the "no" families the full
node-by-node integral is retained. {#tbl-genlik-reduction}

The theorem then says: choose the one function $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}$, and the entire aggregation,
integration, and inference pipeline of Chapters 20 to 24 runs unchanged.

::: {#thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr}
## General-likelihood ML-NMR
Let $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\boldsymbol\theta)$ be any individual-level conditional likelihood (a density
or probability mass in $y$ for each value of the conditional parameter $\boldsymbol\theta$), and let the
network model determine the conditional parameter of an individual with covariates $\mathbf{x}$ in study
$j$ on arm $k$ through $\boldsymbol\theta=\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$, built from the
linear predictor $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd). Then:

1. **(IPD arm.)** For an IPD arm with observed covariates, the arm log-likelihood is the sum of
conditional contributions,
$\sum_{i}\log\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\big(y_{ijk}\mid\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}_{ijk};\boldsymbol\xi)\big)$.

2. **(AgD arm.)** For an AgD arm with $n_{jk}$ (possibly reconstructed) observations and unobserved
covariates distributed as $f_j$, the arm likelihood is the integrated likelihood
$$
\bar L_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{jk}}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}
\big(y_{ijk}\mid\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)\big)\,f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-genlik-general}
each factor a well-defined likelihood contribution by @thm-marginal-individual-likelihood, the product
justified by @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood, and the integral computed by the Sobol' QMC rule of
Chapter 22.

3. **(GLM reduction.)** If $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\theta)$ is a one-parameter GLM density with mean
$\theta=g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$ and the kernel is affine in $\theta$ for each fixed $y$, then
@eq-genlik-general reduces to the mean-aggregation model of @thm-aggregation with aggregate mean
$\bar\theta_{jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))f_j(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$. The affine-in-$\theta$
hypothesis is essential and restrictive: it holds for the Bernoulli mass, but *not* for the Gaussian
density, the Poisson mass $\theta^{y}e^{-\theta}/y!$, the survival kernel $h^{\delta}S$, or the
proportional-odds mass $p_k$, all of which are nonlinear in $\theta$ and retain the full integral
(@tbl-genlik-reduction). So "reduces to a GLM" really means "reduces in the Bernoulli case"; a reported
continuous arm mean is instead modeled directly through its exact aggregate mean on the identity link.

4. **(NMA reduction.)** If there are no covariates (or $f_j$ is degenerate at a single $\mathbf{x}_j$),
@eq-genlik-general reduces to the standard network meta-analysis likelihood (@thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma).

In particular @eq-genlik-general accommodates survival outcomes with
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}=h^{\delta}S$ (@def-censored-likelihood) and ordered categorical outcomes with
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}=p_k$ (@def-proportional-odds), as well as continuous, binary, count, and negative
binomial outcomes, by changing only the integrand $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1* is the definition of a likelihood from conditionally independent observations: with covariates
observed, individual $i$ contributes $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_{ijk}\mid\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}_{ijk};
\boldsymbol\xi))$, and conditional independence makes the arm likelihood the product, hence the arm
log-likelihood the sum.

*Part 2* is @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood with the conditional kernel
$L_{i\mid\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol\xi;y_{ijk},\mathbf{x})=\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_{ijk}\mid
\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi))$. Each factor is well defined and finite by
@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood: for a probability-mass kernel $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\in[0,1]$ the
integral is at most $1$, and for a density kernel it is the marginal density of $Y_{ijk}$, finite for
almost every value. The QMC evaluation is the Sobol' rule of @thm-hypercube-integration applied to the
nonnegative integrand $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_{ijk}\mid\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};
\boldsymbol\xi))$, with the covariate marginals mapped by @thm-inverse-cdf and the dependence supplied by
the Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-sklar).

*Part 3.* Suppose $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\theta)$ is, for each fixed $y$, an affine function of the mean
$\theta$, say $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\theta)=A(y)+B(y)\,\theta$. With $\theta(\mathbf{x})=
g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$ and $\bar\theta_{jk}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_{jk})f_j$,
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\big(y\mid g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))\big)f_j(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}=A(y)\!\int\! f_j+B(y)\!\int\! g^{-1}(\eta_{jk})f_j=A(y)+B(y)\,\bar\theta_{jk}
=\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\bar\theta_{jk}),
$$
so the integrated likelihood equals the kernel evaluated at the aggregate mean $\bar\theta_{jk}$, which is
the mean-aggregation model of @thm-aggregation. (The Bernoulli kernel $\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{1-y}$ with
$y\in\{0,1\}$ is affine in $\theta$, equal to $\theta$ when $y=1$ and $1-\theta$ when $y=0$, so binary
ML-NMR is the canonical instance.)

*Part 4.* If there are no covariates, $\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)=
\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi)$ is constant in $\mathbf{x}$, the integral over the (degenerate)
$f_j$ is the integrand itself, and @eq-genlik-general becomes $\prod_i\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_{ijk}\mid
\boldsymbol\theta_{jk}(\boldsymbol\xi))$, the ordinary arm likelihood of a network meta-analysis on the
chosen scale; the network reduces to the no-regression case of @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma.

The survival and ordinal instances are immediate: substitute $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(t,\delta\mid\mathbf{x})=
h(t\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta}S(t\mid\mathbf{x})$ from @def-censored-likelihood, or
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(k\mid\mathbf{x})=p_k(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)$ from @def-proportional-odds, into
@eq-genlik-general. Neither kernel is affine in a single mean, so neither reduces under Part 3; the full
integral is retained and computed by QMC. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Cost, and why it is the price of generality.** The simple picture first: for each aggregate patient we
