compute the outcome likelihood at $N$ representative covariate values and average them, and we redo this
every time the sampler proposes new parameters. Everything after this sentence is detail. The integrated
likelihood @eq-genlik-general is evaluated at $N$ Sobol' nodes for each AgD observation at every Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo leapfrog step (Chapter 24). For survival there is a second integral hidden inside each node: computing
$S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-\int_0^t h)$ at a flexible baseline hazard requires integrating the hazard over
time. The cost is therefore $N$ covariate nodes times a time quadrature times the number of observations
times the number of gradient evaluations; this is the heaviest computation in the book, but it is linear
in each factor and entirely parallelizable, and it is what buys an outcome-agnostic method. The
diagnostics of Chapter 24, $\widehat R$ (@thm-gelman-rubin), effective sample size (@def-mcmc-ess), and
the integration-error monitoring of @def-integration-error-monitoring, govern both the Markov chain and
the QMC truncation; model comparison across competing likelihoods (a Weibull against an M-spline baseline,
proportional odds against multinomial) uses the information criteria of @thm-dic-waic-loo and the
Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out of @def-psis-loo. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**One family at a time, or a joint network?** A natural question is whether a single network may combine
survival, ordinal, binary, and count outcomes. Two readings, both supported by the framework. The common
case in this book is one outcome family per network: every study reports the same endpoint, one kernel
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}$ is used throughout, and the machinery is reused across outcome families only in the
sense that different networks plug in different kernels. The framework also permits, in principle, a single
joint model whose studies report *different* outcome families, provided they share the treatment-effect
parameters $\gamma_k$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ on one common linear-predictor scale: then study $j$
contributes its own kernel $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}^{(j)}$ but the same $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$, and the shared
estimand is the relative effect on that scale. What makes such a combination meaningful is precisely a
shared linear-predictor-scale effect; without it there is nothing to pool. Unless stated otherwise, the
networks in this book use one family at a time. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Generality as the distinguishing feature.** This theorem is the structural reason ML-NMR is more
flexible than its competitors. Matching-adjusted indirect comparison (Chapter 18) and simulated treatment
comparison (Chapter 19) need a separate weighted or standardized estimator for each outcome type, and each
compares only two trials. General-likelihood ML-NMR changes one function, $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}$, and reuses
the entire aggregation, integration, and inference pipeline across a whole network.
The same generality carries to the unanchored extension ML-UMR (Chapter 26), where the time-to-event and
proportional-odds kernels reappear inside the unanchored likelihood (@thm-mlumr-tte). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This capstone corresponds to J.8 in the proof catalogue.

## A fully worked survival example {#sec-genlik-example}

We carry a complete survival aggregation from a conditional hazard model to an aggregate-data likelihood,
choosing the numbers so that every survival probability, marginal hazard, restricted mean, and likelihood
factor is exact and checkable by hand. The example uses a single binary covariate, which turns every
covariate integral into a two-point sum (the degenerate QMC rule for a Bernoulli marginal) and makes the
non-collapsibility of the hazard ratio and the collapsibility of the RMST visible in closed form. It is a
stylized analogue of the multiple-myeloma progression-free-survival network of @phillippo2025general,
whose `multinma` analysis integrates several covariates over Sobol' nodes with a Gaussian copula; here we
keep one binary covariate so the arithmetic is transparent.

::: {#exm-genlik-survival}
## Exponential-hazard aggregation with a binary prognostic covariate
This is the full computation promised for the running trial of @exm-genlik-running; it takes that trial from
the conditional hazard model to the aggregate-data likelihood. A target population $\mathcal{P}$ (the
comparator AgD population) has a single binary prognostic covariate
$X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=1)=q=\tfrac12$; $X$ marks a high-risk subgroup. The outcome is time to progression,
modeled with a constant (exponential) conditional hazard. The control treatment $C$ has
$$
h_C(s\mid x)=\lambda_x,\qquad \lambda_0=1,\quad\lambda_1=3\quad(\text{events per year}),
$$
so the high-risk group has triple the control hazard. Treatment $A$ acts by proportional hazards with a
covariate-independent conditional hazard ratio $\psi=\tfrac12$ (a beneficial treatment, conditional log
HR $=\log\tfrac12=-0.693$, no effect modification),
$$
h_A(s\mid x)=\psi\,\lambda_x=\tfrac12\lambda_x .
$$
By @thm-survival-hazard-relation the conditional survival functions are
$S_C(s\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x s}$ and $S_A(s\mid x)=e^{-\psi\lambda_x s}=e^{-\lambda_x s/2}$.

**Step 1: marginal survival.** Averaging over $X$ (a two-point sum, weights $\tfrac12,\tfrac12$),
$$
S_C^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\tfrac12 e^{-s}+\tfrac12 e^{-3s},\qquad
S_A^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\tfrac12 e^{-s/2}+\tfrac12 e^{-3s/2}.
$$

**Step 2: the marginal hazard ratio is time-varying (@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying).** Using
@lem-survivor-weighted-hazard, $h_C^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=(e^{-s}+3e^{-3s})/(e^{-s}+e^{-3s})$ and
$h_A^{\mathcal{P}}(s)=\tfrac12(e^{-s/2}+3e^{-3s/2})/(e^{-s/2}+e^{-3s/2})$. The conditional hazard ratio is
the constant $\psi=0.5$ at every time and covariate; the marginal hazard ratio
$\mathrm{mHR}(s)=h_A^{\mathcal{P}}(s)/h_C^{\mathcal{P}}(s)$ is not:

| $s$ (years) | $h_C^{\mathcal{P}}(s)$ | $h_A^{\mathcal{P}}(s)$ | $\mathrm{mHR}(s)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ | $2.0000$ | $1.0000$ | $0.5000$ |
| $0.5$ | $1.5379$ | $0.8776$ | $0.5706$ |
| $1$ | $1.2384$ | $0.7689$ | $0.6209$ |
| $2$ | $1.0360$ | $0.6192$ | $0.5977$ |
| $4$ | $1.0007$ | $0.5180$ | $0.5176$ |
| $\infty$ | $1.0000$ | $0.5000$ | $0.5000$ |

At $s=0$ no selection has occurred and the marginal hazard ratio equals the conditional value $0.5$; for
every $s>0$ it exceeds $0.5$, attenuated toward the null $1$, peaking near $0.62$ around one year before
the slow ($x=0$) stratum comes to dominate both risk sets and the ratio returns toward $0.5$. A single Cox
fit reporting "$\mathrm{HR}=0.60$" would be reporting an artifact of the one-year follow-up window, not the
conditional effect $0.5$. (Check the $s=0$ entry by hand: $h_C^{\mathcal{P}}(0)=(1+3)/2=2$ is the average
baseline hazard, $h_A^{\mathcal{P}}(0)=\tfrac12\cdot 2=1$, ratio $0.5$.)

**Step 3: RMST is collapsible (@thm-rmst-collapsible).** Take horizon $\tau=2$ years. The conditional
RMSTs are $\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid x)=\int_0^{\tau}e^{-\lambda_x^{(t)}s}\,ds=(1-e^{-\lambda_x^{(t)}
\tau})/\lambda_x^{(t)}$ with $\lambda_x^{(C)}=\lambda_x$ and $\lambda_x^{(A)}=\tfrac12\lambda_x$:
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_C(2\mid 0)=1-e^{-2}=0.8647,\quad
\operatorname{RMST}_C(2\mid 1)=\tfrac{1-e^{-6}}{3}=0.3325,
$$
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_A(2\mid 0)=\tfrac{1-e^{-1}}{0.5}=1.2642,\quad
\operatorname{RMST}_A(2\mid 1)=\tfrac{1-e^{-3}}{1.5}=0.6335 .
$$
The marginal RMSTs computed two ways agree exactly. Averaging the conditional values:
$\operatorname{RMST}_C^{\mathcal{P}}(2)=\tfrac12(0.8647+0.3325)=0.5986$ and
$\operatorname{RMST}_A^{\mathcal{P}}(2)=\tfrac12(1.2642+0.6335)=0.9489$. Integrating the marginal survival
of Step 1: $\int_0^{2}(\tfrac12 e^{-s}+\tfrac12 e^{-3s})\,ds=\tfrac12(1-e^{-2})+\tfrac16(1-e^{-6})=
0.5986$, the same. The collapsible RMST contrast is
$\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{CA}^{\mathcal{P}}(2)=0.9489-0.5986=0.3503$ years, equal to the average of the
conditional contrasts $\tfrac12(0.3995+0.3010)=0.3503$. Unlike the hazard ratio, this marginal contrast is
the average of conditional contrasts.

**Step 4: the marginal individual likelihood (@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood).** The comparator study
reports its covariate distribution ($X\sim\operatorname{Ber}(\tfrac12)$) and supplies, on the control arm,
reconstructed pseudo-IPD; take two pseudo-observations, an event at $t_1=0.5$ ($\delta_1=1$) and a
right-censoring at $t_2=2$ ($\delta_2=0$). With the conditional censored kernel
$L_{i\mid x}=h_C(t\mid x)^{\delta}S_C(t\mid x)=\lambda_x^{\delta}e^{-\lambda_x t}$, the marginal
contributions are the two-point sums
$$
L_1(\boldsymbol\xi)=\tfrac12\big[\lambda_0 e^{-\lambda_0 t_1}\big]+\tfrac12\big[\lambda_1
e^{-\lambda_1 t_1}\big]
=\tfrac12 e^{-0.5}+\tfrac12\,(3e^{-1.5})=0.3033+0.3347=0.6380,
$$
$$
L_2(\boldsymbol\xi)=\tfrac12\big[e^{-\lambda_0 t_2}\big]+\tfrac12\big[e^{-\lambda_1 t_2}\big]
=\tfrac12 e^{-2}+\tfrac12 e^{-6}=0.06767+0.00124=0.06891 .
$$
($L_1$ is a density, with units of inverse time; $L_2$ is a probability.) Here the two integration nodes
are the covariate values $\{0,1\}$ with QMC weights $\{\tfrac12,\tfrac12\}$; a continuous covariate would
replace this exact two-point rule with an $N$-node Sobol' average, as in the `multinma` analyses.

**Step 5: the aggregate arm likelihood (@thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood).** The product over the two
pseudo-observations is
$$
\bar L_{C}(\boldsymbol\xi)=L_1(\boldsymbol\xi)\,L_2(\boldsymbol\xi)=0.6380\times 0.06891=0.04396 .
$$
This is the contribution of the comparator control arm to the network likelihood at the parameter values
$(\lambda_0,\lambda_1)=(1,3)$; as a function of the unknown $\boldsymbol\xi$ it is
$\bar L_C(\boldsymbol\xi)=\big[\tfrac12\lambda_0 e^{-\lambda_0/2}+\tfrac12\lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_1/2}\big]
\cdot\big[\tfrac12 e^{-2\lambda_0}+\tfrac12 e^{-2\lambda_1}\big]$ (each bracket is $L_1$ and $L_2$ rewritten
as functions of the free rates, using the observed times $t_1=\tfrac12$ and $t_2=2$: the first factor
carries $e^{-\lambda_x t_1}=e^{-\lambda_x/2}$, the second $e^{-\lambda_x t_2}=e^{-2\lambda_x}$), ready for
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The
treatment arm contributes the analogous product with $\lambda_x$ replaced by $\psi\lambda_x$, tying the
arms together through the shared $\psi$ exactly as the anchored network requires. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the example shows.** The conditional model is as clean as a GLM: a constant hazard ratio $\psi=0.5$,
linear on the log-hazard scale, identifiable from any arm. Yet the marginal hazard ratio is time-varying
(Step 2), so it is not a transportable parameter; the RMST contrast is collapsible (Step 3), so it is a
faithful read-out in a stated population but, by the scale-misalignment remark after
@thm-rmst-collapsible, still requires the target covariate distribution to transport. The aggregation
itself (Steps 4 and 5) is exactly the integrated likelihood @eq-genlik-general with $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}=
h^{\delta}S$, computed as a finite sum because the covariate is binary. Replace $h^{\delta}S$ by the
proportional-odds mass $p_k$ and the same five steps deliver the ordinal aggregate likelihood; this is the
generality of @thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr made concrete. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-genlik-notes}

The general-likelihood ML-NMR framework of this chapter is the contribution of @phillippo2025general,
which extends the original binary and count ML-NMR of @phillippo2020mlnmr to survival, ordered
categorical, and other outcome types through the integrated likelihood @eq-genlik-general, and is
implemented in the `multinma` package. The survival development, the proportional-hazards and
accelerated-failure-time individual models, the flexible M-spline baseline hazard, and the
reconstruction of pseudo-IPD from published Kaplan-Meier curves, follows @phillippo2025general and Chapter
7 of @phillippo2019thesis. The survival fundamentals of @sec-genlik-survival, the survival function, the
hazard, the identity $S=\exp(-\int h)$, and the right-censored likelihood under independent censoring, are
classical; the standard reference is @klein2003, and the independent-censoring factorization
@prp-censored-likelihood-density is the textbook construction. The Kaplan-Meier reconstruction algorithm
is due to @guyot2012; its role in the unanchored network is developed in Chapter 26
(@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction).

The non-collapsibility of the marginal hazard ratio (@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying) is a much-discussed
feature of survival analysis: even a correctly specified conditional proportional-hazards model induces a
marginal hazard ratio that varies with time and is attenuated toward the null, because the at-risk set is
selected by survival. The survivor-weighted representation @eq-genlik-survivor-rep and the exponential-tilt
covariance argument given here make the attenuation precise and quantitative; the phenomenon is the
survival-scale instance of the general non-collapsibility of @def-non-collapsibility (Chapter 7) and of
the odds-ratio non-collapsibility of Chapter 11, and it is the reason the restricted mean survival time
(@def-rmst), collapsible by the Fubini argument of @thm-rmst-collapsible, is increasingly preferred as a
marginal summary. The transportability subtlety, that RMST collapsibility does not imply RMST
transportability when the conditional model is on the log-hazard scale, is the scale-misalignment finding
analyzed for the unanchored case by @chandler2025mlumr and revisited in Chapter 26 (@thm-mlumr-tte); the
clean transportable object remains the conditional log-hazard model under conditional constancy of
relative effects (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) of Chapter 17.

The proportional-odds model (@def-proportional-odds) is the standard cumulative-logit model for ordered
categorical data; the validity lemma @lem-ordinal-valid-probabilities and the proportional-odds
interpretation are elementary and appear in any categorical-data text, with @mccullagh1989glm the classical
GLM reference. The aggregation theorems @thm-marginal-individual-likelihood and
@thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood are the general-likelihood forms of the mean-aggregation theorem
@thm-aggregation of Chapter 20, and they inherit the numerical-integration apparatus of Chapter 22, the
Sobol' net (@def-sobol-net, @thm-hypercube-integration, @sobol1967), the inverse-CDF transform
(@thm-inverse-cdf), and the Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-sklar, @sklar1959). The
Bayesian computation, including the diagnostics and model comparison referenced in @sec-genlik-general, is
the Stan/Hamiltonian Monte Carlo apparatus of Chapter 24 (@carpenter2017stan), and the network reductions
to standard NMA (@thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma) connect to @dias2018nma.

There is no machine-checked counterpart for this chapter: the companion Coq development does not
formalize survival, hazard, restricted mean survival time, or ordered categorical outcomes, whose content
needs Lebesgue integration over time beyond the machinery used elsewhere in the development. The results of
this chapter are pen-and-paper, and the proofs above are self-contained. This chapter
corresponds to results J.1 (survival function), J.2 (hazard), J.3 (the identity $S=\exp(-\int h)$), J.4
(the right-censored likelihood, with J.4a the conditional hazard ratio, J.4b the time-varying marginal
hazard ratio, and J.4c the collapsible RMST), J.5 (the marginal individual likelihood), J.6 (the aggregate
arm likelihood), J.7 (the proportional-odds model), and J.8 (the general-likelihood framework) of the
proof catalogue in `proofs/J_general_likelihoods.md`.

## Exercises {#sec-genlik-exercises}

The exercises progress from warm-up and interpretation to computation and proof. A star ($\star$) marks an
exercise whose full worked solution appears in Appendix F. Start with the first two if the formal
development felt fast: they use only the running trial and the definitions.

::: {#exr-genlik-hazard-not-probability}
**(Warm-up: hazard is a rate, not a probability.)** In the running trial (@exm-genlik-running) the control
hazard is the constant $\lambda_0=1$ per year for standard-risk and $\lambda_1=3$ per year for high-risk
patients. (a) Using $S(t\mid x)=e^{-\lambda_x t}$, compute the probability a standard-risk control patient
is progression-free at $t=1$ and at $t=2$ years. (b) Do the same for a high-risk patient. (c) A colleague
says "a hazard of $3$ per year means a $300\%$ chance of progressing in a year, which is impossible." In one
or two sentences, explain what is wrong with this reading and what the number $3$ actually measures.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-cond-vs-marg-interpretation}
**(Interpretation: conditional versus marginal hazard ratio.)** The running trial has conditional hazard
ratio $\psi=0.5$ at every time and covariate value, yet the marginal hazard ratio in @exm-genlik-survival
rises to about $0.62$ near one year before falling back. (a) State in one sentence which of the two,
conditional or marginal, is the transportable estimand the network reports, and why. (b) Using the
risk-set-drift table in @sec-genlik-hazard-ratio, explain in plain language why the treated arm retains
relatively more high-risk patients at later times. (c) A submission reports a single "HR $=0.60$" from an
unadjusted Cox fit with two years of follow-up. Explain why this number should not be read as the
per-patient effect of treatment.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-weibull-hazard}
**(Computation) Weibull from the hazard.** Let the conditional hazard be the power law
$h(s\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,\nu\,s^{\nu-1}$ with shape $\nu>0$ and scale
$\lambda(\mathbf{x})>0$. Using @thm-survival-hazard-relation, compute the cumulative hazard
$H(s\mid\mathbf{x})$, the survival function $S(s\mid\mathbf{x})$, and the density $f(s\mid\mathbf{x})$, and
verify that $f=h\,S$. Show that with $\nu=1$ the model is exponential. Then write the right-censored
individual likelihood @eq-genlik-censored-lik for an observation $(t,\delta)$ and confirm it reduces to a
density when $\delta=1$ and to a survival probability when $\delta=0$.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-cumulative-hazard-additive}
**(Computation) Additivity of the cumulative hazard under PH.** Under the PH model @eq-genlik-ph with a constant
baseline hazard $h_{0j}(s)=\kappa_j$, show that the conditional cumulative hazard is
$H_{jk}(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\kappa_j t\,\exp(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$ and hence
$S_{jk}(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-\kappa_j t\,e^{\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})})$. Deduce that on the log
cumulative-hazard scale, $\log H_{jk}(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\log(\kappa_j t)+\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})$, so the
covariate effect is additive and time-invariant. Explain why this makes the conditional log hazard ratio
@eq-genlik-cond-loghr time-invariant but does not make the marginal hazard ratio time-invariant.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-binary-reduction}
**(Proof) Binary ML-NMR as a special case.** Take $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y\mid\theta)=\theta^{y}(1-\theta)^{1-y}$
with $y\in\{0,1\}$ and $\theta=\operatorname{expit}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x}))$. Using
@thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr part 3, show that the integrated marginal likelihood
@eq-genlik-marginal-lik equals $\bar p_{jk}^{\,y}(1-\bar p_{jk})^{1-y}$ with $\bar p_{jk}=\int
\operatorname{expit}(\eta_{jk})f_j$, and that the aggregate arm likelihood for an event count $r_{jk}$ out
of $n_{jk}$ is the binomial kernel $\bar p_{jk}^{\,r_{jk}}(1-\bar p_{jk})^{n_{jk}-r_{jk}}$. Contrast this
with the survival kernel $h^{\delta}S$ and explain precisely why the latter does not collapse to a
function of a single aggregate mean.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-ordinal-network}
**(Computation) A three-category proportional-odds likelihood.** Let $K=3$ with cutpoints $\alpha_1\le\alpha_2$ and
linear predictor $\eta$. Write the three category probabilities $p_1,p_2,p_3$ from @eq-genlik-po-prob
explicitly in terms of $\operatorname{expit}$, verify directly that they are nonnegative and sum to one
(@lem-ordinal-valid-probabilities), and compute the marginal individual likelihood of an AgD observation
$y=2$ when $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=1)=q$ and $\eta(x)=\gamma+\beta x$, as the two-point sum
$q\,p_2(1)+(1-q)\,p_2(0)$. Numerically evaluate it for $\alpha_1=-1,\alpha_2=1,\gamma=0.5,\beta=1,q=0.4$.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-mhr-attenuation}
**($\star$, Challenge) Quantifying the attenuation.** In the frailty setting of @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying with a binary
frailty $\rho(X)\in\{\rho_0,\rho_1\}$, $\rho_0<\rho_1$, $P(X=1)=q$, constant baseline $h_{a0}(s)=1$, and
constant conditional hazard ratio $\psi\in(0,1)$, derive a closed-form expression for the correction
factor $R(s)$ in @eq-genlik-mhr and hence for $\mathrm{mHR}(s)$. Prove that $R(s)\ge 1$ for all $s$ with
equality only at $s=0$ and as $s\to\infty$, that $\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi$ on $(0,\infty)$, and that
$\lim_{s\to 0^+}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\lim_{s\to\infty}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi$. Identify the time of maximal
attenuation by setting $\tfrac{d}{ds}R(s)=0$ and interpret it as the moment of maximal survivor selection.
(This generalizes the table in @exm-genlik-survival, recovered at $\rho_0=1,\rho_1=3,q=\tfrac12,
\psi=\tfrac12$.)

*Hint.* With a binary frailty the survivor covariate density is a two-point distribution, so write $R(s)$
as a ratio of two tilted two-point means and use the exponential-tilt identity from the proof of
@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying. The maximizer of $R(s)$ solves a transcendental equation; identifying it
qualitatively, as the time of maximal spread between the two survivor distributions, is enough for the
interpretation.
:::

::: {#exr-genlik-rmst-transport}
**($\star$, Proof) Collapsible but not transportable.** Consider two populations $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{P}^{*}$
with the same binary covariate $X$ but different prevalences $q\ne q^{*}$, and the exponential PH model of
@exm-genlik-survival (conditional hazards $\lambda_x$ for control and $\psi\lambda_x$ for treatment, shared
across populations: conditional constancy of relative effects holds on the log-hazard scale). Using
@thm-rmst-collapsible, show that the RMST contrast $\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{CA}(\tau)$ differs between
$\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{P}^{*}$, and give an explicit formula for the difference in terms of
$q-q^{*}$. Conclude that RMST collapsibility (a within-population identity) does not imply RMST
transportability (a cross-population identity), and explain how this differs from the conditional
log-hazard model, which is shared across the two populations by assumption. Relate your conclusion to the
scale-misalignment remark following @thm-rmst-collapsible and to Chapter 26 (@thm-mlumr-tte).

*Hint.* By @thm-rmst-collapsible each population's RMST contrast is a weighted average of the two
conditional contrasts with weights $(1-q,q)$; subtract the two averages, the conditional contrasts cancel,
and the difference is a single multiple of $q-q^{*}$. The two-population snapshot in @sec-genlik-rmst is the
numeric special case.
:::
